speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a point of privilege which stems from the passage yesterday of the resolution preceding the bill to amend the Bank Act. As you will recall, Your Honour, this was passed yesterday. I discovered that within minutes the press gallery had copies of this bill; not only copies of the bill, but a precis of the salient points. I myself have not yet received a copy of the bill, and when I telephoned this morning to try to get a copy I was told that while there were some copies they were being reserved for certain individuals, and were not available for members of parliament.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this is an intolerable affront to members of parliament, and I for one do not propose to submit to it.

The second aspect of this policy pertains to future arrivals and those persons now in Canada who do not apply for permanent residence on or before July 25, 1966. The applications of such persons for landing will be approved only if:
(a)	They are not within the prohibited classes described in the Immigration Act;
(b)	they have not gained admission by any fraudulent means;
(c)	they do not have immigrant applications pending when they come to Canada;
(d)	they apply before the expiry of their period of authorized stay and have not violated the conditions of their entry; and
(e)	they come within one of the two following categories:
(i) those who would be acceptable as unsponsored immigrants if applying as such abroad; or
July 8. 1966

(ii) those who were, before admission, the spouses or minor children of citizens or legal permanent residents of Canada.
To deter those who might deliberately use this method of gaining admission rather than applying for immigrant visas at immigration missions abroad, the actual granting of permanent resident status to these persons will be deferred for one year from the date their applications are conditionally approved. Approval will be revoked if, during this period, there is definite evidence of criminal or other tendencies which establish that the applicant is undesirable as a future Canadian citizen.
Those applicants who fail to comply under this policy will be asked to leave Canada voluntarily, failing which deportation action will be initiated. Should parliament approve the bill to establish an immigration appeal board which is now before the house, persons ordered deported will have the right of appeal to an independent, judicial body which, in all but a limited number of exceptional cases, will have the power to deal conclusively with their appeals, subject only to a further appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.
The third and most important aspect of this policy consists of better controls to prevent recurrence of the present situation. The new policy will be widely publicized in Canada and abroad to ensure that persons in Canada and the travelling public are well aware of our laws and requirements. A better documentation system for visitors will be instituted to identify visitors and to verify their departure without burdening them with undue formalities. Other improvements will be made in the internal methods of the department to enable efficient detection, apprehension and deportation of those who violate the conditions of their stay.
This new policy will apply to all categories of non-immigrants, except students and seamen who will continue to be governed by special policies and procedures. I would also like to emphasize that the procedures I have outlined affect only those who seek to migrate to Canada outside the proper channels. The qualified migrant seeking admission to Canada in the legal manner will not encounter any barriers. Nor do we intend that the new procedures will impede international travel or cause delays at Canadian ports of entry.

I also wish to announce, Mr. Speaker, that the government intends to introduce as soon

as possible revised regulations governing the admission of persons sponsored by relatives in Canada. The proposed changes will remove all discrimination on grounds of geographic or ethnic origin of immigrants-

Mr. Speaker, the problem of the illegal entry of persons circumventing our immigration laws is not a new one, but recently it has grown very greatly both in volume and in intensity. With the general principles enunciated by the minister this morning it would be difficult to quarrel, but I confess that I do have mixed feelings-yes, grave qualms-about the interpretation and enforcement of those principles. A great deal more will have to be known about the actual procedures which are proposed by the department before a final judgment on the new policies can be rendered by the house. I am by no means sure, after listening to the minister this morning,

July 8. 1966
Immigration
that he has solved the headaches either for the department or the individuals concerned.
Personally, sir, I believe that the first principles ought to be generosity and sympathetic understanding to those already in the country who can meet health, security and crime free standards. This country can afford some genuine humanitarianism in its immigration laws. My own conclusion is that only a full amnesty for those already in the country is a realistic solution at this time, coupled with a clear enunciation of the principles to be followed in the future in dealing with illegal entrants and the adequate and uniform enforcement by the department and the new immigration appeal board of those principles.
I confess that I had some particular concern about what the minister said in relation to those who come to the country in the future as visitors and who seek to remain. He said they would be admitted if they would have been accepted as unsponsored immigrants or if they were spouses or minor children of citizens or of legal permanent residents of Canada. Later on the minister said there would be a complete revision of the regulations dealing with sponsorship, and he did say that a broader range of relatives than at present would be included.
Let me say I had an ominous feeling that in this particular first sentence the minister was giving us a forerunner of his intentions and that he might be about to adopt the proposals made by Mr. Joseph Sedgwick, Q.C. as to restrictions on sponsored immigrants. If he were to do that I think he would strike terror in the hearts of many immigrants. The minister shakes his head. Let me say to him that I believe this is part of the policy which ought to be clarified at the time he is bringing forward his white paper. There is no reason why these proposals related to persons entering on non-immigrant visas should be confined to those who are spouses and minor children.
The minister in his statement said the policy for the future will remove all discrimination on the grounds of geographic or ethnic origin of immigrants. I remind him that basically that was the policy and regulations laid down in 1962.

Mr. Speaker, I should like my words to be an unqualified and warm welcome of this announcement. I think the minister and his advisers are to be congratulated on the improvements and steps forward that are embodied in these proposals. We in this party have for many years, to my knowledge, advocated three basic changes in the act and the administration of the regulations. We have advocated the elimination of all racial discrimination; we have advocated that the problem of visitors who seek to stay in Canada be dealt with properly, and we have advocated fair hearings for those who seek admission to Canada.
Dealing with the first point about the elimination of racial discrimination, we warmly welcome the statement of the minister. The regulations which were introduced-apparently the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) has forgotten this-during the time of the previous administration expressly contain discrimination in respect of the sponsorship of would-be immigrants to Canada. I have the regulation in front of me, and it provides
July 8. 1968

far stricter rules in regard to those who come from Asia and Africa than in regard to those who come from Europe or the United States. I was glad to hear the minister say in his statement that this discrimination is to be eliminated.
Mr. Speaker, I remind the minister, although it is not appropriate that he should deal with it now, that there remains in the Immigration Act the explicit authority to the governor in council to discriminate on the basis of ethnic origin. This authority is contained in section 61 of the Immigration Act. I call upon him to follow up what he has done so far by assuring us that we in this house will be invited to remove from the Immigration Act the authority given by parliament to discriminate on racial grounds.
The next point deals with the question of visitors. We welcome two aspects of this measure as mentioned today. The first is that those who come in through the lax application of the administration will be given a chance to show that they are qualified to stay in Canada, and that their suspense in this regard will be relieved.
I merely wish to point out one detail, and perhaps this is a matter that has been overlooked. The minister in his statement said that those who were in the prohibited classes described in the Immigration Act would not be entitled to have their applications approved. I remind the minister that the Immigration Act includes, in paragraph (t) of section 5, a prohibition against admission of anyone who does not comply with the regulations, so every single one of these people in theory could be eliminated under this general description on the ground that, for example, they had not complied with the regulations because they did not have immigrant visas. I ask the minister that the absence of an immigrant visa, which has been frequently used in the past as an excuse, without any reason given for refusal of admission, will not be used in denying admission to those who will apply under this proposal and who are now in Canada. Indeed, I hope this method of dealing with applications will not be followed at all.
[DOT] (11:40 a.m.)
I want to tell the house and the minister that despite these improvements there remains a procedure applied by the department which is dangerous and vicious; that is to say, that those who apply to come can be
Immigration
excluded, not because of any specific objection but because they have not got an immigration visa, which the department has refused to give without telling the applicant why. This is unjust. It is wrong. It is a practice that is being carried out now, and I urge the minister to review it.
Last is the question I mentioned before, namely that of providing fair hearings for all applicants. The whole immigration appeal procedures which have been brought forward in the bill which has been given first reading in this house are immensely improved by the proposed legislation, in that an independent appeal tribunal will be set up. But this will be meaningless unless it is made perfectly clear that the objections to the admission of an immigrant are made known to the applicant, so his hearing before the immigration appeal board and the special inquiry officer is meaningful and not just a hearing with regard to a piece of paper which the department decided the immigrant should not have.
I am also glad to hear that the question of security procedures with regard to immigrants from eastern Europe is to be reviewed. For a long time we have had a ridiculous situation in this regard whereby, for example, 400,000 people emigrated from Yugoslavia to West Germany, France and other parts of western Europe and made a tremendous economic contribution to those countries; yet we were told in Canada that because our security procedures did not enable us to look into the cases of people who came from a country such as Yugoslavia, they could not be admitted, as though some security risk existed in bringing in a few skilled people to Canada from Yugoslavia, which security risk did not exist at all in West Germany and other parts of western Europe.
I am delighted to hear that changes are to be made in this field. I would be less than generous if I did not say that after years of waiting for some action in this regard we are delighted to see that we are moving in the right direction. We will wait for the white paper. We want the committee to go into this matter thoroughly. There are many other things in the Immigration Act that require changing, but at last we are on the move.

As the Prime Minister indicated, I think the day before yesterday in answer to a question, Canada of course is in favour of such a conference as is proposed, providing it can be arranged. For some months now we have been engaged in talks with other countries in trying to bring about the calling of a conference. We have had discussions with the government of India, the government of Poland, the government of Britain and a representative of the Soviet union. Only this week I have had a discussion with a high personage in the government of the Soviet union here in Ottawa with regard to this matter.
If it is possible for present objections on the part of one of the co-chairmen to the calling of such a conference to be overcome, I am sure this would be welcomed all over the world. I believe there are some very difficult impediments in the way. If they were removed Canada, of course, would be happy to support that course.
With regard to whether I would be prepared to go to the Soviet union, I can say we have had some discussions here in Ottawa recently about this matter, and I do hope to go to the Soviet union some time later.

speechtext:
A telegram was sent to me by the president of the Canadian Labour Congress dated July 6. It reads:
As indicated to you during negotiations concerning the International Longshoremen's Association I wish to reiterate to you that as a firm matter
7388	COMMONS
Inquiries of the Ministry of policy the Canadian Labour Congress is unalterably opposed to any type of legislation indicating compulsory and binding arbitration. This type of legislation is completely contrary to democratic methods and to normal collective bargaining.
Claude Jodoin, President C.L.C.
An identically worded night letter or telegram was sent to the Prime Minister. The reply I sent to the president of the C.L.C. on behalf of the Prime Minister and myself reads as follows:
In reply to your telegrams of July sixth to the Prime Minister and to me I would say that the traditional opposition of organized labour and management to the practice of compulsory arbitration in disputes over interests as distinct from grievances affecting rights is well known and I appreciate and respect the basic considerations underlying this attitude. It is equally well known and documented in the settlement of some disputes that labour and management have resorted to arbitration on specific issues that cannot be settled otherwise and which stand in the way of complete settlement. Likewise labour and management have agreed to settlements which provide for binding arbitration within prescribed limits. Previous governments of Canada have enacted legislation providing for binding solutions. As you are well aware most of the issues involved in the recent longshore dispute were settled by agreement and those directly concerned realized that legislative action was necessary and was promised to solve the remaining issues and thus bring about a complete settlement.
There is ample proof of this fact. As one instance, you will recall that on June thirteenth while you were present the Prime Minister read a statement to the ILA representatives concerning the two or possibly three issues remaining in dispute in which he suggested that the ILA drop its demand for the application of retroactivity to overtime and that the shipping federation accept the following proposal with respect to the four-hour recall "that this item be submitted to the commission for examination and that the recommendation of the commission with respect to this item be binding in precisely the same way as the recommendation with respect to gang-size. The four-hour recall would then be dealt with and included or not within the contract in the manner specified by the commission". You will also recall that also in your presence the suggestions of the Prime Minister in this regard were later accepted by both parties.
John R. Nicholson, Minister of Labour.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, July 5, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-207, to authorize the making of contributions by Canada toward the cost of programs for the provision of assistance and welfare services to and in respect of persons in need-Mr. MacEachen-Mr. Batten in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
When the committee rose last Tuesday we were about to discuss clause 5.
July 8, 1966

On clause 5-Amount of contributions.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is one of the important clauses of this bill. In fact it is the one which sets out the formula under which contributions will be made to the provinces on the one hand with respect to assistance payments made by them and on the other hand with respect to the costs of welfare services maintained or established by the provinces. It would be useful if the minister would make a statement giving the terms of the formula in simpler language than is contained in the clause.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in response to the question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I shall begin to reply, and if he wishes further information I shall be glad to try to provide it. The rate of contribution for assistance, which is referred to in paragraph (a), is set out at 50 per cent of the cost to a province and to municipalities within the province. Federal sharing is limited to expenditures made by a province and municipality, although if a voluntary agency provides assistance that assistance will be supported by the federal government only in respect of that portion of the cost paid by the province or one of its municipalities. This gives an opportunity for voluntary agencies to participate in the plan.
Paragraph (b) provides a basis of contribution toward welfare service costs. It is divided into two parts which set out alternative methods by which the federal government may make contributions to a province at the option of the province. Under either alternative 50 per cent is the rate of sharing by the federal government.
During discussion of the Canada Assistance Plan at the conference of welfare ministers early in the year there was some consideration of how we might be able to participate, in as administratively simple a manner as possible, in sharing in the additional new service costs incurred by a province. As hon. members will note, in one case the federal government will pay additional amounts incurred by a province over and above the costs incurred by it and its municipalities for welfare services during a defined base period. The base period is set out in subparagraph (B)(1) as the cost to the province coinciding with or ending in the period commencing April 1, 1964, and ending March 31, 1965. In that case there will be the use of a base period. In the second case there is not the use of a base period but simply a cut-off point, which is March 31, 1965.
Canada Assistance Plan
In a sense this really is not a crucial point to the principle of the bill. It provides some administrative flexibility to the provinces. In the second case, by using a cut-off period the province of Quebec in particular felt it would be more simple administratively and would not involve as great a federal involvement in ascertaining their actual costs under this program.
Provinces may choose either option. Indeed, they may choose a combination of both options. There is the 50 per cent generally. Then there are the two alternative methods for meeting the additional costs of welfare services and then, of course, there is the method of dealing with regulations for the determination of capital costs which generally will be excluded from federal financial support.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
I agree with the minister that there is nothing crucial with respect to the alternative choices granted to the provinces in subparagraph (B), and I am not going to suggest there is something crucial with respect to the rest of the clause, but I would like to be sure that we clearly understand it. In clause 5 we are dealing with two main areas in which contributions will be made by the federal government. One is in the area of what is called assistance, actual dollars that are paid to people in need. The other is in the area of welfare services, people put on staff to render services even though some of those services may get through in terms of equivalent dollar value to people.
Is it clear with respect to the first category, that of assistance payments to people, that the federal government will pay 50 per cent of whatever is the total cost to the province, municipality, or any other approved body? Does the minister want to say yes at this point?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Yes.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext: In respect of what are defined as welfare services and with regard to the putting of people on staff and providing services, the federal government will not pay a portion of the amount the provinces or municipalities have been spending up to the base year but rather will pay 50 per cent of the excess of cost from then on?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
That is right, Mr. Chairman. Naturally the provinces would have preferred that we pay all costs. The purpose,
July 8, 1968

Canada Assistance Plan however, really is to provide an incentive to the provinces to engage the additional personnel who will be required to make the Canada Assistance Plan work along the lines expected. We expect that incentive is provided by sharing one-hall of the cost of additional staff according to either of the options set out in the clause.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
May I pursue this a moment
longer. I thank the minister for his statement and I welcome the suggestion that this is set up as an inducement to the provinces to expand their welfare services. I take it that this is in line with the view generally expressed that we want not only to make dollars available to people by way of assistance but also want to help people get off welfare as fast as they can.
I do not wish to get into a matter of detail at this time which would interfere with general discussion by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa and the hon. member for Simcoe East, but at some point I should like to have two breakdowns in respect of the total amount of money the government expects to pay in the first year under the provisions of clause 5. My two breakdowns are these: On the one hand I should like to know how the $85 million which the minister is talking about is broken down among the various categories under which these moneys will be paid. My second request is for a breakdown with regard to how much of the $85 million would be under the heading of assistance and how much would be under the heading of welfare services. If my friends wish to pursue a more general discussion before we get into this detail I do not mind, but at some point I should like to have these detailed figures put on the record.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister whether the federal government takes any part in the establishment of regional offices. Could he also outline to us where these regional offices are, particularly with regard to my own province of Ontario? Does the federal government have any part in the choosing of the regional offices? I am asking this question because in the province of Ontario regional offices are now being established. In the areas where regional offices are being established now does the federal government pay 50 per cent of the cost of operation and of staff?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the location of any regional office which is set up

under the Canada Assistance Plan would be,
as the hon. member for Simcoe East appreciates, a matter for decision by the provincial governments, but we will be sharing through the federal parliament, if this bill is approved, 50 per cent of the additional staff costs in any office.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether the minister grasped the last part of my question. Will the federal government pay 50 per cent of the total cost of the operating
staff of the regional office?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
We pay 50 per cent of the
staff salaries.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to
follow up this line of questioning. I believe I understand the clause correctly, but perhaps the minister would be able to define again the actual participation of the federal government in the payment of services so far as existing offices are concerned. As the minister has defined, and as it states in the clause, I know that any extension of services will be met by a 50 per cent contribution from the federal government, but if there is no extension and merely a salary increase, let us say, will the salary increase also be covered by the 50 per cent formula?
Second, in the event that there is no extension of services or even a salary increase, the municipality or agency will not benefit through the Canada Assistance Plan unless it does extend its services. Is that correct? I am not saying this in a negative sense because I agree there is an incentive here. When I spoke on this bill earlier I deplored the lack of standards. Perhaps it is a better way if the plan is providing incentives to improve standards.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
With regard to the first question concerning whether salary increases aside from staff additions would be supportable, the answer is yes, if the province selects option 5(l)(b)(i)(A). My hon. friend asks whether there is any way in which welfare services can be supported except in the case of an extension. Welfare services can be supported if these welfare services are purchased under the definition of assistance in clause 2, welfare services purchased by or in the name of a provincially approved agency. In other words, 50 per cent will be shareable if these services are purchased for recipients of social assistance or public assistance. To that extent, the existing welfare services will
July 8, 1966

be supported under the Canada Assistance Plan.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext: I have one follow-up question. I agree that services and direct assistance are supportable but there seems to be no provision for capital cost support. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
This is correct. In clause 5 the right to assistance does not include any capital cost as defined by regulation for the purpose of this paragraph. The general effect of the paragraph is to exclude capital expenditures from the calculation of the costs of assistance. There may be some exceptions to this and we will deal with these exceptions by way of regulations. For example, another step may be taken by the parliament of Canada with regard to old age security recipients which will considerably influence the extent of provincial supplementation necessary or desirable. Whether old age pensioners receive $100 a month or $105 or an even higher amount under other old age income security programs, it seems to me there will still be a need for the kind of supplementation that is provided under the Canada Assistance Plan.
For example, I mentioned, or I had intended to, the cases of elderly people who may be in special care homes, the monthly cost of which may be $300. The Canada Assistance Plan has a role, it seems to me, over and above any other flat rate income program, so under the Canada Assistance Plan the federal government will be doing its part in sharing in the cost of supplementation. The federal government will share half the cost of supplementation, but we do not intend to place any upper limit on this federal share as it relates to income maintenance payments or health and welfare services. Since both traditionally and constitutionally the responsibility for persons in need of assistance rests with the provincial governments, the federal government cannot go much farther than this.
The federal government, of course, has made additional funds available to the provinces through action with respect to old age security programs and has indicated to the provinces our expectation that these funds would be used in supplementary and other assistance payments and welfare services. It is estimated that in 1966-67 the provinces will save $12.3 million through a reduction of the age eligibility from 70 to 69 and having that group of the population removed from the old age assistance case load. This figure will rise substantially until, by 1970, the provinces will be relieved entirely of their share of the cost of old age assistance, with a saving we estimate in that year of approximately $50 million. The sharing of the existing provincial costs of mothers' allowances and child welfare will, of course, provide the provinces with another source of additional new revenues, not only to improve these programs but also to provide funds for improvements of other aspects of their assistance programs, including supplementation.

July 8, 1966

the end of four years the Governor in Council can terminate the agreement into which the province and the federal government have entered, what will be the result? I would think that if the provinces felt there was any danger that at the end of four years the whole responsibility with respect to programs which they would build up in this period would be landed in their laps, they would approach welfare programs with much more caution than if they could be assured that the plan was likely to be a continuing one.

I think the minister is aware that provincial governments are always reluctant to commit themselves to expenditures in conjunction with the federal government if they feel that at some time or other they may be left holding the bag.
We have had some experience of this. Some years ago we started a physical fitness program. The federal government suddenly decided to withdraw from it. The provinces had one of two alternatives, either drop the physical fitness program entirely or pick up that share of the cost which the federal government had dropped. The program I have referred to was not a very big one, and therefore it had nothing like the significance of the program about which we are now talking. Nevertheless, the fact must be considered that by the end of four years the federal government's contribution under this program will be very considerable. If the provinces felt that they were at all likely to be left with the entire burden of implementing the program outlined here, I think they would be very reluctant to expend moneys on the program at the rate that we all hope they will be expended.

speechtext: This is intended to cover Indians who are living on crown land or on land without municipal organization. subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext: What is the difference between the situation of those who have moved off a reserve into non-organized territory and those who have moved into municipally organized territory?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext: If Indians move into a municipality and live there, they become integrated within the population, and they receive welfare assistance on the terms applicable to every other resident. The whole purpose of part II of the bill is to provide a basis, through agreements, by which the federal government will participate in bringing normal welfare services to the Indian population. In other words this paragraph which defines "Indians" indicates a group for whom higher rates of contribution will be available under the Canada Assistance Plan.

The transferring of administrative responsibility for the provision of welfare services has been discussed at various meetings with the provinces. Under the cost sharing formula set out in the draft agreement the provincial and federal governments would share the cost of assisting Indians under part II on a matching basis up to the per capita level of cost incurred for assisting the non-Indian population in the province. speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of Amateur Sport
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PROGRAM TO ASSIST PERSONS IN NEED
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, part III, work activity projects, provides a basis for future contributions toward projects designed to provide work orientated activities for persons who are not able to take advantage of normal employment, vocational training or rehabilitation opportunities. This type of program has been requested by several provinces which feel that a new factor is required in their programs.
Under clause 14 (a) projects are defined in terms of the purposes for which they are to be set up. Their objective will be to prepare for entry or return to employment persons who, because of environmental, personal or family reasons, have unusual difficulty in obtaining or holding employment, or taking advantage of training or rehabilitation programs. Many of those involved will be persons who have a history of chronic dependency because of a variety of problems which, it is felt, can best be dealt with under a welfare system.
It should be emphasized that a significant distinction of a work activity project is that it is a social service relating to trade or work, so that a participant and his family will receive counsel and support in order that the family will be strengthened by assistance to the head of the family whose employability is a difficulty. In essence, the purpose of this project is to provide appropriate training and work activity for persons who can take advantage, and whose dependency may be decreased or whose employability may be enhanced. This is an experiment and involves new territory.

Some of the cases mentioned by the hon. member may involve special training or placement efforts, and this can be provided through other programs. The real purpose of this provision is to support work activity projects which will enable persons to enhance their employability. It applies not only to those persons but to projects which are designed for individuals such as the severely retarded, whose limited employment potential can be enhanced if they are given some form of meaningful activity.
It is envisaged that this type of activity for the severely retarded will be given under conditions of sheltered employment, so there is that aspect to the plan. An example of one kind of work project can be found in the re-establishment centres operated by the national assistance programs in Britain. In the main, the types of persons referred to these centres are those receiving assistance, who have been continuously unemployed for a long time-in some cases a year or more-and those who have in consequence lost the habit [DOT]of work and have become unaccustomed to the ordinary daily routine which is the pattern of the life of a man or woman in regular employment.
In the United States a program similar to this envisaged under the work activity projects takes the form of community work training programs under the social security act, and work experience programs under the income opportunities act. In both cases the programs are operated on a federal-state basis and administered by the department of health, education and welfare. In the United States over $100 million is being expended this year for this kind of program. Canada is now moving into this field by the provisions in this part of the bill.

We look forward, now that discussion on the Canada Assistance Plan bill is drawing to a close, to the minister's producing his blueprint so long promised, in connection with the wider field of rights and privileges for the older people of this country. Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party may I say at this point that, as we said at earlier stages with respect to this legislation, we welcome this bill and are glad to vote for it. As we made clear at the earlier stages of debate, we see in this legislation provisions that improve the administration of social welfare in Canada. We have spelled that out in some detail, so that it is not necessary to do so on third reading.
However, it is still our view that it was a bitter disappointment that when this legislation was brought in it failed to meet the hopes which the minister and other members of the government had held out to our older people for over a year, indeed for 14 months. We have been told for a long time that the Canada Assistance Plan was legislation under which, amongst other things, there would be improvements with respect to the pensions of our retired Canadians. It turned out that there was no such provision in this legislation, and we have drawn attention to that fact as forcefully and as energetically as we could.
I think it would be appropriate to say that this is another example of the value of parliamentary debate. During the course of it, it is quite obvious that the government has got the message and has come to the realization that it cannot leave our old age security recipients relying on the provisions of the Canada Assistance Plan for increased pension income. It is obvious that the government has come to the realization that it has to do something else. That is why we debated this measure as we did.
I think it was a shameful performance for the people of this country to be led for three or four days to believe that the minister would make a statement on this matter at the end of second reading, a statement which he then refused to make. But that is now part of history. What is significant today is that the minister has assured the house and the country that before this session recesses a statement by the government will be made in the

house telling us what the government's plans are with respect to old age security recipients. He not only gave that assurance on orders of the day this morning but he alluded to it half a dozen times when we were in committee of the whole today.

However, in the intervening months the stand taken by President Johnson to all intents and purposes seems to have taken on the same considerations incident to, and part of, the policies advocated by Senator Gold-water. What information was given to Canada in this regard?
Certainly the decision to take that course was a new initiative. It implied the adoption of a hard line by the administration of the United States. The result has been that fear has touched the hearts of men everywhere. No longer is there any question that what is taking place is the waging of a war. What has been the reaction of the Soviet and Chinese communist leaders? Up to the present it has been described as cautious. For how long will that attitude be maintained by the communist countries?
The United States is pouring out its gold and its blood on behalf of the maintenance of freedom for us all. Will this new phase bring about an alteration in the powers of resistance of North Viet Nam, or will it have the result of uniting the communist nation, alienating the friends of the United States in all parts of the world, and finally bringing about a challenge to world peace? We have a right to know where the government of Canada stands. We have a right to suggest that the concealment of Canada's position behind a barrage of words is not an answer to the Canadian people.
In the latter part of June the Secretary General of the United Nations set forth certain basic principles as being appropriate to a peaceful settlement. The first was the cessation of bombing in North Viet Nam. His suggestion in that regard was met by intensification and an expansion.
The second was the scaling down of action in South Viet Nam. His expressed hopes that this might be done had been answered by the North Vietnamese by an ecceleration of infiltration into South Viet Nam.
The third point was that there should be inclusion in the talks that will take place of all who are actually fighting there, meaning that the Viet Cong should have representation at any conference. The last of these three points seems to be a reasonable one, a necessary one, one that should be generally acceptable.

This is not an easy matter. I am deeply concerned about the events of the last few days. So that there may be no mistake as to what I mean, I refer to the intensification and expansion of bombing. But we do ourselves injustice as a nation if, having those ideas, we proceed to wide condemnation of the United States and its policies. I disagree strongly with the latest initiative. I find it difficult to understand how, in the light of the experience of history, a nation can believe that however powerful its bombing capacity may be, it can destroy the fortitude and determination of a people. I think Canada should make it abundantly clear to the United States that this is the view of Canadians as a whole regarding this recent venture into extended bombing. Taking this stand however, we should not, as a nation, with the freedom of all mankind dependent on the United States and its forces, engage in the easy course of condemning without offering an effective alternative.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to assure my right hon. friend that there has not been, and will not be, any concealment of Canada's position with regard to this matter, but in my official capacity I have to determine, together with my colleagues, the circumstances and the occasions when we, too can enjoy the same freedom of exposition which rests with those who do not have the immediate responsbility of deciding the course that Canada must take in this or any other international matter.
I have examined the debate in the British House of Commons. I have read carefully what the Prime Minister of Britain said yesterday, and what Lord Home said yesterday, and I suggest to hon. members that there has not been, in any free parliament that I know of, more questions answered about this particular problem. While hon. gentlemen
Interim Supply
may complain about the generality of some responses, I suggest if they will examine the responses made by other foreign ministers they will find that Canada has been as forthcoming as she has a right and a responsibility to be at this time in regard to a matter, which the right hon. gentleman said, is one that gives him great concern, as it does all of us.
Of course I am aware that there is widespread concern here, and among Canadians generally, about the most recent course of developments in Viet Nam. The right hon. gentleman spoke of the speech made the other day by Lord Avon, the former British Foreign Secretary. Lord Avon was not referring to the current situation in Viet Nam. He was dealing with what he thought would be a desirable ultimate solution, a solution not unlike the proposition which the prime minister and I have put forward on two occasions, once in the house and once in the external affairs committee, as to what the ultimate disposition might be of this problem.
But we are addressing ourselves today not to what is going to happen when the conflict is over, but to how we are going to bring this conflict to an end, and to what we can do to realize this objective, and to what our view is about what is alleged to be a recent escalation in the pattern of war carried on by the United States against North Viet Nam.
Let there be no doubt we are all concerned about this problem. On a number of occasions the government has expressed its reservations with regard to the bombing of North Viet Nam and about the whole sequence of events which led the United States to the conclusion that it had no option but to adopt this course. I made my views known before the recent bombings took place, and in a manner which I believe was the most effective way to engage in consultations with a country with which Canada has such close ties.
One could be dramatic. One could engage in particular public postures that might bring acclaim, but I want to say that as long as I am Secretary of State for External Affairs, and certainly with regard to this situation, 1 am going to carry on in the way which I believe will most likely yield favourable results, rather than seek acclaim by some public position that is not capable of yielding a satisfactory solution.
The Prime Minister made clear on June 29 that we would be glad to see the bombing stopped, that we would be glad to see the

July 8. 1986
Interim Supply
infiltration of North Vietnamese troops into South Viet Nam stopped, and that we would be glad to see unconditional negotiations for peace started. This has always been our position. We urged a ceasefire before the President of the United States said he was prepared to enter into peace talks without any preconditions. When we now urge a ceasefire we must take into account some of the implications which were mentioned yesterday by Mr. Wilson. We could have talks if the parties were so disposed, without waiting for a ceasefire, and these talks in turn might lead to a ceasefire.
I think it important that we understand fully the implications of the action which has now been taken to bomb the oil storage facilities in North Viet Nam. I do not think we can limit our analysis merely to the military aspects of this operation. I propose to go beyond these aspects, to go into other implications which seem to me essential to a full appreciation of the present situation.
So far as the strictly military aspects are concerned, it can be argued that the general pattern of activity has not been significantly altered by the bombing of the oil storage facilities of North Viet Nam. On the understanding that has been communicated to me, it is not the intention of the United States government to extend the bombing to targets which are not directly related to the infiltration of men and supplies from North Viet Nam to buttress the insurgency in the south.
The fact is that the oil storage facilities which have been the target of recent attacks are located in close proximity to major concentrations of population in North Viet Nam.
I take it from the preliminary reports that have been made available to the government of Canada that every care has been taken to spare civilian life in those operations. Nevertheless I would be less than frank if I did not say there is a risk inherent in these operations in terms of giving this conflict a character, a complexion which I am sure all of us would be concerned to avoid, and which my right hon. friend himself said he was concerned to see avoided.
There is a further aspect to these latest operations which is bound to cause concern. That is the possibility, as my right hon. friend mentioned, of a greater engagement in this conflict by those who have supported and actively encouraged the policies and the efforts of the government of North Viet Nam. It is not possible, I think beyond a certain 
point, to estimate what the threshold of that greater engagement may be, but it must be clear that everyone in every country, in all of the continents, is concerned about the dangers flowing from any change in the pattern of the present conflict.
It seems to me exceedingly difficult to guarantee against a miscalculation on the part of one or other of the powers concerned who may consider the course of developments in Viet Nam as carrying a direct risk to their national security. All I can say at the moment is that, from all the information that has been made available to us, there appears to be a continuing recognition of the need for restraint on the part of all the governments directly concerned in the conflict.
I wish to deal with a matter which seems to me to be crucial from the point of view of the Canadian government and of other governments which believe that a negotiated solution is the right way of resolving the Viet Nam conflict. The question we must ask ourselves is whether these latest developments, or any future developments tending in the same direction, are likely to help or hinder the prospect of such a solution. This has been the cornerstone of Canada's policy and the guiding consideration in the efforts which we have been making in recent months.
I am bound to say on balance, that whatever the rights or wrongs of the situation may be, it is the judgment of the Canadian government that there is a relationship between this whole matter of bombing and the prospects of arriving at even a beginning of a process which might in due course yield an honourable accommodation of the interests of the major parties in the conflict in Viet Nam.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I should like to take this point a little further by explaining to the house the positions of the government of North Viet Nam and the government of the United States, as I understand them, on the basis of what has been said publicly and in private discussions. The government of North Viet Nam has called for a permanent and unconditional cessation of all bombing and other acts of war against their territory. This is one of the elements in a letter which president Ho Chi-Minh addressed to the Prime Minister on January 24, and in the absence of which the government of North Viet Nam does not appear prepared to envisage a political solution. The argument behind this formulation is that by bombing targets in North Viet Nam
July 8, 1966

the United States is encroaching on the sovereignty of that country, and that this is a violation of accepted standards of international law and international relations. The government of North Viet Nam accordingly does not think that a willingness to cease this bombing should be qualified by any conditions whatsoever, or that it warrants any countervailing undertakings by the North Vietnamese government in respect of its own policies.
I think the North Vietnamese point of view is well reflected in a statement issued by the Chinese authorities in Peking on July 3 last. The following extract is relevant to this matter:
U.S. imperialism long ago completely violated the Geneva agreements and broke the line of demarcation between South and North Viet Nam. It has now further broken this line by its bombing of the capital of the heroic Vietnamese people. The United States must be held responsible for all the serious consequences arising therefrom. With the breaking of the line of demarcation by the United States, the Vietnamese people have ceased to be subject to any restrictions.
This is a significant statement. The house will note that it refers twice to the demarcation line which, however temporary it was designed to be, was laid down in the Geneva cease-fire agreement of 1954. The statement appears to argue that, so long as this agreement has not been superseded by a permanent settlement of the whole Viet Nam question, that line must to all intents and purposes be regarded as a de facto political boundary between North and South Viet Nam, and must be respected as such.
This interpretation of the provisions of the Geneva agreement is, I think, one which Canada, as a member of the international Commission in Viet Nam is bound to take seriously. It is also, I think, an interpretation which lies at the root of the whole position of the government of the United States as regards the matter of support and sustenance which the government of North Viet Nam has afforded to the insurgency in the South. I regret to say, however, that it is only partially accepted in the statement from which I have read to the house. For, having placed due emphasis on the inviolability of the line of demarcation between South and North Viet Nam, the Chinese statement goes on to say that "all support and aid rendered by the North Vietnamese people to South Viet Nam are within the sacred right of the Vietnamese people". It is this evident inconsistency which is the crux of the problem we are facing in Viet Nam and to which we must address
Interim Supply
ourselves if there is to be any prospect of a peaceful and lasting settlement of the present conflict.
What is the position of the government of the United States? It is in the following terms as they have been given to us. The United States is prepared to stop the bombing of North Viet Nam at any time as part of a mutual reduction of hostilities on both sides. They regard the military activities in North and South Viet Nam as forming part of a single problem. If the North Vietnamese were prepared to respect the demarcation line in terms of the assistance they are providing to the insurgency in the South, the United States, for their part, would be prepared to match such a move by halting the bombing of targets in the north which are associated with that assistance.
This, then, is the impasse as I see it. There is a relationship between this matter of bombing and whatever moves it may be possible to make toward an eventual settlement.

speechtext:
If it is not that report, I do not know what report it is. When the question was directed to me I assumed it must be that report. I do not know of any other such report in respect of Laos in recent months.
The North Vietnamese government believes that the bombing of their territory should be stopped by a unilateral commitment on the part of the United States. The United States government, on the other hand, argues that it is unrealistic to expect them to give a unilateral commitment of this kind which would leave North Viet Nam without any commitment in respect of their infiltration of men and supplies into the south.
What is to be the position of the Canadian government in this situation? I believe that there are two choices open to us. We can take strong public positions on any or all of the issues involved in the present conflict. That is the easiest thing we can do. Alternatively, we can continue to do what we have been trying to do. So long as I am in this office that is what I propose to continue to do, because I believe this is the only effective way available of achieving the objectives we have in mind. We will continue to conduct quietly and through diplomatic channels our efforts to find the basis for an accommodation in Viet Nam.
I would seriously suggest to the house that we can follow one or the other course I have mentioned. We cannot effectively follow both at one and the same time. I think we have to admit to ourselves that there are no simple solutions to this conflict. And, because there are no simple solutions, a settlement in Viet Nam will not be achieved overnight; it can only emerge from a patient probing of positions.
e (4:50 p.m.)
It will have to go right to the roots and the origins of the conflict in Viet Nam and it will have to be such as to hold out an assured prospect of peace and stability, not only in Viet Nam but in Southeast Asia as a whole. This is what Lord Avon had in mind when he talked of neutralization; not now, not as a meand to bring this conflict to an end, but as the kind of solution that would follow a negotiated settlement. If this is what we are

working toward, then I think it will be agreed we must take first steps first.
It is being put to me from time to time that Canada, either by itself or in co-operation with other countries, should issue a call to a new Geneva conference. Before we set out to determine the proposed new role for the commission, we had already done that. Before we sent Mr. Ronning to Hanoi and Saigon and elsewhere we had already done that. I now resist this course, not because it is unreasonable or because it does not represent a long-term objective of the government of Canada. We have had discussions with the government of India, and I mention India because of the speech made yesterday by her distinguished prime minister to the effect that there should be a conference called.
This proposal was made over a year ago and again last November before we contemplated the proposed role for the commission, and before we decided on the Ronning missions. I have now resisted this course, in the sense that I have resisted it before, because all the information available to me indicates that a call of this kind will not have the desired results in present circumstances, much as I would like to be able to say that the situation was otherwise. We have been told this without going to Moscow, on the highest authority. It is one thing to call for a conference; it is quite another thing to ensure its being attended by those who must be there.
It seems to me that a conference lies at the end of the road, not at the beginning. If one could be held now, and if the Soviet union, as co-chairman, acquiesced in the suggestion of the prime minister of India to join with Britain in calling such a conference, all of us would support this. But I would have to say, as I have already implied, that knowing what I do I would be greatly surprised if the representations that must be at such a conference would be prepared to attend one at this time, whether it would be on Viet Nam or indirectly on Laos or Cambodia.
Do you mean Russia or the United States?
I prefer to leave my statement as it is.
It is ambiguous.

It is not ambiguous.
I cannot foresee what intermediate steps may have to intervene before the time for such a conference is ripe. But, on the basis of
July 8, 1966

all the discussion we have had, it is my assessment that it is likely there would have to be some preliminary undertakings, and I emphasize the word "undertakings", about the points of substance which are at issue in this conflict. What this means, in Canadian terms, is that we must do all we can to try to create the conditions in which the processes which will lead to an ultimate settlement can be started. This is precisely the task to which we have addressed ourselves.
I say again that we welcome the proposals made yesterday by the Prime Minister of India. The purposes and objectives behind her proposals are shared by the Canadian government and they are shared by all of us in this house. If these proposals commend themselves to the parties concerned, and if the parties concerned would attend the conference-I am sure the United States would be among those that would-and if progress on that basis were possible, I can assure the house and the government of India that Canada is prepared to do whatever may be required of us to see that these proposals are translated into action.
My right hon. friend spoke of Mr. Ron-ning's two visits to Hanoi. I would like to underline certain aspects of this initiative which may have been lost sight of in the great volume of publicity, and on this I regret to disagree with my right hon. friend, which Mr. Ronning's visits have generated.
First, I have said that this was a Canadian initiative and that it was carried out by Mr. Ronning on the instructions of the Canadian government, and not on the instructions in any way of any other government. I reiterate this today because the impression has been created in some quarters that Mr. Ronning's mandate may have been something other than it was.
Second, I would like the house to understand that the assignment we have taken on is essentially in the nature of a good offices assignment. It is inherent in such an assignment that we would be concerned to understand the positions and attitudes of all the parties, and that we would do our best to interpret and clarify the positions and attitudes of one side to the other. That, broadly speaking, has been the form which Mr. Ronning's assignment has taken.
Third, I would like to restate the ultimate object of this initiative. It has seemed to us that if a beginning is to be made in the long and patient process which we hope will lead to ultimate peace in Viet Nam, we must find
Interim Supply
a basis on which both sides would be prepared to see such a beginning made. The mere calling of a conference, desirable as that is, does not meet this essential objective, as we have learned in our discussions with both sides. This is the only potentially useful channel through which there has been contact with both sides in a long time. I will not say it is the only channel, but it is the only channel which has access to both sides. I regard this as a tribute to our country as well as to Mr. Ronning himself.
I do not wish to give the house a misleading impression of our results so far. We have not achieved any spectacular results and I think I can quite frankly say that we have had no illusions as to the pace at which progress was likely to be possible.
As I have explained previously to the house, we regard the two visits which have now been made to Hanoi-there may be others -as phases of a continuing effort. Over how long a period of time this effort may extend I cannot say. What is significant is that we have had a fair hearing, and on both occasions with the top personalities of the north and the south and, of course, with the government of the United States. I can say that if the channel we have established remains open, and if its potential usefulness is not called into question by any of those concerned, I do not think, in a situation where a failure of communication may be crucial, we can discount the significance of such a channel for the time when the circumstances for the solution of the Viet Nam conflict are ripe.
The situation facing us in Viet Nam is as serious as any which has faced us since the Korean war. Since that time there has been growing confidence on the part of the international community that it has the means of bringing its influence to bear on situations of this kind, and to put an end to armed conflict, and to lay the groundwork for political solutions. That is the essence of the concept of peacekeeping which Canada and others have tried to develop and strengthen through the United Nations.
We accepted the suggestion of the president of the United States that he would welcome any effort by any country to try and bring about at least preliminary talks that might lead to serious negotiations, which in turn might result in a negotiated settlement. It was in the light of this situation that we thought last December there was a role for the international commission. Canada, India and Poland, as members of this commission,

July 8, 1966
Interim Supply
have had experience in Indochina now for 11 years. Being the only body that has a continuing link with Hanoi and Saigon we thought that, quite apart from any authority given to that commission under the Geneva agreement, it might undertake the effort to try and bring about a narrowing in the position taken by the various parties.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
To that end we have had useful and fruitful exchanges with India and Poland. Our view was that the time had come to use the commission for this purpose. We did not suggest they were not as sincerely interested in peace as we were. One of the countries took the position that perhaps this was not the particular moment in which to establish a role for the commission as a mediating instrument. But we continue, all of us, India, Poland and Canada-and this was rearffimed yesterday by the Prime Minister of India-to look upon the commission as having a role in this situation.
The government of India reaffirmed yesterday that they would be happy to see the commission used to try and bring the parties together. Because we felt there would be some delay in trying to use the commission for the purpose I have mentioned, the government asked Mr. Ronning, a man born in China, who speaks Chinese, who knows many of the personalities involved, to undertake, if this could be arranged with the support of the governments	concerned-the	United
States, North Viet Nam and South Viet Nam-a series of discussions to find out if there was a basis for a preliminary discussion between the parties.
We have made a commitment, and we intend to respect it, to the parties concerned that what went on in Hanoi is a matter that must rest with the government of Canada until such time as we are in a position to report, finally, success or failure. It cannot be any other way. My hon. friend the member for York South the other day asked me whether I was in favour of the three proposals made by the Secretary General of the United Nations. He knows my views in these matters; he has known them for a long time. He knows where I stand and where this government stands. But if I had replied in specific terms to that question, I would have violated a commitment which Mr. Ronning, speaking for the government of Canada, made in discussions he has had. I do not propose in any way to endanger or destroy the credibility of a channel that is still open,

and which may yet be used to deal with this very serious situation.
We have had discussions only this week with representatives of the government of the United States, right here in Ottawa. I have had discussions, as the Prime Minister has, with the Deputy Premier of the Soviet Union who is visiting Canada. We will continue these discussions next week. Other countries are engaged in similar processes. I want this house and the country to know that there is no item on our agenda that is more important than trying to bring about some process of discussion between the parties concerned, in order that we can bring an end to the conflict in Viet Nam. That is the objective of all of us.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that a military solution of this problem of course is not possible by itself. We are all aware of the dangers that flow from the conflict that has raged in that area. We are dealing with the situation as it is now; we are not dealing with its genesis. We have sought not to emphasize the history of this situation, but to try and see if we could not make our position as a mediator more effective by taking the most objective position possible. I think thus far we have succeeded in doing this.
I can tell the house that no opportunity will go by without our making every attempt that we can, by ourselves, as a member of the commission or in concert with other countries, to try to bring about peace talks. When they do take place, whether by a Geneva conference or as a result of the kind of situation that developed in Korea and Malaysia, namely by gradual process, then we will address ourselves as one country in the international community to those methods by which we hope to bring about an effective neutralization of the whole area.
The objective that Lord Avon spoke of the other day will not be achieved without, of course, the use and support of the international community, through the United Nations or otherwise. Mr. Chairman, I resume my seat after saying that this undoubtedly is one of the most serious situations the world faces. It is not a conflict in which we are engaged. Mr. Chairman, I think it is appropriate on interim supply that the committee should take some time to discuss the very serious situation which has developed in Viet Nam. I have listened with great interest to the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I must say that about all the minister has done has been to tell us about all the difficulties there are. He has given no leadership whatever, nor has he set forth any program which the government intends to pursue with a view to finding a solution to the unfortunate debacle in Viet Nam.
We have waited now for three years to get some statement of policy from the government. All we have had in three years, and again today, has been a series of platitudinous bromides calculated to put the house to sleep and to lull the fears of the Canadian people. Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, the fears of the Canadian people cannot be lulled quite so easily. The recent escalation of the bombing to include the areas of Hanoi and Haiphong has touched the conscience of the world. World leaders, some of whom had in the past supported United States intervention in Viet Nam, have now spoken out with alarm at this most recent escalation of the war.
The fact is that by this recent step, the government of the United States is now gambling with human survival and is, step by step, bringing this conflict to the place where it will inevitably spread into what may be a major world war. The President of the United States has been assuring his people that there really is not anything to worry about, that the Chinese will not react very violently, and that the main thing to do is to get the war in Viet Nam finished before the November elections. It almost seems as if the President has succeeded in brainwashing the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who referred today to the recent escalation of bombing as an alleged escalation of bombing.
Well, Mr. Chairman, there does not seem to have been merely an alleged-and I put the "alleged" in quotes-escalation of the bombing. The bombing has now been brought to

the capital city and to the chief port of North Viet Nam, and dangerously close to the borders of mainland China. If this process of escalation continues, it can only be a matter of time until mainland China becomes militarily involved. In an appearance before a congressional commission General John P. Lavelle, on March 5 said that American military forces had all their plans laid by which they could easily bomb the major centres of mainland China. He said there really was not anything to be concerned about if mainland China entered the war. What we have to ask ourselves is, after we have bombed the main centres of China where does the United States go from there?
[DOT] (5 .20 p.m.)
You cannot defeat a country just with air raids. If the United States seeks to land troops in mainland China and becomes involved in a land war with 700 million people, it would be like a fly on flypaper. Not only will it be involved in Asia, with a billion Asiatics violently hating the white man foi the barbarous bombing of Asiatic communities, but if the United States becomes involved in a war with mainland China it will have to blockade China and insist thal Canada stop trading with China, and that we do not feed the people of China. If anyone if so naive as to believe that the United States would continue to allow Canada to send wheat to China, I am sure that they are due for a very rude awakening.
Whether or not the military intervention o: mainland China will bring the Soviet Unioi into such a conflict, we do not know; but we do know that this most recent escalation hai probably brought the world closer to a majo: world war than anything which has happenee in the last 21 years.
We have made no secret of where we ii this party stand. We have said all along tha we believe that the United States has n< business in Viet Nam; that she is there ii violation of the Geneva accord agreement that she is there in violation of the charter o the United Nations. The only possible solutioi is, first, for the United States to discontinu the bombing unconditionally; second, th United States should be prepared to treat nc only with North Viet Nam but also with th national liberation front in South Viet Nan Third, the United States must be prepare to withdraw its forces, to be replaced by peacekeeping force; to give to the people c Viet Nam an opportunity to decide in supervised, secret ballot whether or not the

want to unite North and South Viet Nam; and to determine the kind of government which they shall have. That has been our position, and it has not altered.
The Leader of the Opposition said that our position has not been the same as the position taken by the prime minister of Great Britain, and that is true. I have differed with Prime Minister Wilson, both publicly and privately, on this question. However, I would point out that even Prime Minister Wilson, who has up until recent days supported the position of the United States, has now dissociated himself from the bombing of Hanoi and Haiphong, and has expressed his strong disapproval of this most recent escalation of the war.
Mr. Wilson is not the only one who has altered his position somewhat with reference to the Viet Nam situation. My friends to the right in the Conservative party, who a year ago last May were making speeches completely in support of United States intervention in Viet Nam, are now beginning to have very serious doubts about the long-term effect of that military venture.
This is because what both the official opposition and the government have failed to recognize, Mr. Chairman, is that it is only a difference of degree between bombing the villages and the hamlets of North Viet Nam and then starting to bomb the cities of North Viet Nam. The first step was bound to lead to the next step, just as the step now taken of bombing Hanoi and Haiphong will inevitably lead to a further escalation-either the destruction of the port of Haiphong or the mining of the port, or the destruction of the railway leading into mainland China.
I fear that the United States is making the same mistake which it made in Korea, when the President of the United States and General MacArthur assured the people of that great country that there was no danger in United States troops going up to the Yalu River, and that the Chinese had been so intimidated that they were not likely to intervene. But they did intervene.
Fortunately the world managed to get itself out of that debacle, but I am not so sure that it can get itself out of this one unless the leaders of the western world are prepared to take more forthright and courageous steps than the Canadian government has indicated it is prepared to take today. Mr. Chairman, I will deal with that in detail in a few moments. May I as a preliminary answer say to the minister that of course we agree that any attempts which Mr. Ronning can make to find some basis for agreement are all to the good. But that does not relieve the government of the responsibility which it has to lay out a program, to state its position clearly to all the nations of the world, and to follow that program.
I want to say to the minister that we are in a new age of diplomacy. These are no longer the days of Metternich and Disraeli. We no longer need the diplomacy of Talleyrand-Perigord. It is a new kind of diplomacy and leadership which is needed today. This is not all going to be done behind the scenes; it is going to be done by governments and by men like the Prime Minister of Canada and the Secretary of State for External Affairs giving some leadership among the nations of the world.
That is exactly the point to which I am coming. Canada has always placed as the cornerstone of its foreign policy the effectiveness of the United Nations and the building of collective security as the best means of maintaining world peace. United States intervention in Viet Nam has been carried out in complete defiance of the charter of the United Nations, which requires nations to negotiate their differences and to report immediately to the United Nations any alleged measures of self-defence which they propose to take. The United Nations has been scrupulously ignored and avoided by the United States in this whole sorry mess.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Appeals by the Secretary General of the United Nations, U Thant, have been ignored and brushed off abruptly, and sometimes not too courteously. Recently he set forth a proposed program not too different from that which I suggested a moment ago as a possible basis for a solution. He received no answer at all from the United States. Secretary U Thant has described what is happening in Viet Nam

July 8, 1966
Interim Supply
as the most barbarous war in history. Yet this man who is the spokesman for the United Nations gets no hearing, and no action is taken on the proposals he is making.
When we talk about the idea of collective security, is the United Nations only for small powers? Is it only to be used to police the conflicts in Gaza, or in Cyprus, or only to intervene in Suez? When a great power like the United States or the Soviet Union, or when some other major power is involved, is the United Nations supposed to creep away to a corner and pretend that a war is not taking place?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Of course not.

Yet, this war is going on. The minister says "Of course not". The United Nations should not ignore it, and yet the United Nations has been ignoring it, and the minister has done nothing to take this matter to the United Nations, to attempt to obtain a clear statement of opinion.
