speechtext: Is the hon. member not aware that the Secretary General of the United Nations said last January when the United States took the Viet Nam question to the Security Council, that that was not the place for the Viet Nam question, and that it could only be decided within the framework of a Geneva conference, because the parties concerned were not all members of the United Nations organization. That is why this is not before the United Nations.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has just made an excellent point. Yet, not more than half an hour ago he argued that he was going to resist calling the Geneva powers together for a whole series of reasons. He gave us reasons as to why that course would not succeed. Now he is stating that the United Nations can do nothing.
Having ruled out both these international organizations, what does the minister propose?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We did not rule out the Geneva conference.

I did not interrupt the minister while he was making his statement, and I would appreciate his not interrupting me. May I tell the minister that one of the reasons why the United Nations cannot be effective in coping with this problem is because the nations most vitally involved are not members of the United Nations.
That is right.

And why are they not members of the United Nations? Because the government to which the minister belongs, or governments which have preceded this one have never had the courage to support the admission of mainland China to the United Nations. The minister is still prepared not to support such a measure.

How do you
know?

If the minister is prepared to support that measure I shall sit down now, to give him a chance to make a statement. As a matter of fact, I tell the minister that he will never support the admission of mainland China to the United Nations until the day that the United States government admits that it is prepared to admit mainland China to the United Nations.
That is your view.

That is when the Government of Canada will move on this matter.
Since the United Nations is not able to cope with this problem, by virtue of the fact that some countries most vitally involved are not in its membership, this leaves only one international body that has any hope of resolving this problem. I refer of course to those nations which attended the Geneva conference in 1954 and which signed the Geneva accord. That is why some of us have been urging now for some years that the Canadian government, as a representative on the International Control Commission which was set up by that Geneva conference, should insist upon the reconvening of that conference.
We are playing a ludicrous part in an international farce. We are a member of an International Control Commission on which there are Canadian personnel and on which we have spent millions of dollars. Yet the body that set up that commission has never been reconvened to deal with the report of the commission.

speechtext: Yes it was; in 1962.

I said that the body concerned had met in 1962, having met in 1954.

Yes. Nothing has been done to call the conference together, or to take the recommendations made by the International Control Commission, and to seek to implement them.
In 1962 Canada and India signed a majority report complaining about the violation of the Geneva accord by both sides. Nothing was done about this. Canada has never insisted that something should be done about it. We have reached the stage where we ought either to insist that the two co-chairmen reassemble the Geneva conference, and do something to exercise the authority which that body gave to the International Control Commission, or we ought to ask the commission to absolve Canada of any further responsibilities, and to recognize that that phase of the whole story is at an end.
The minister says that it will not be easy to get the Geneva accord powers together. I suggest that the first thing to be done is for the Canadian government to call on the United States government to unconditionally stop the bombing. Nobody is going to attend a conference while the bombing is going on.
The minister spoke as if he thought it was too much to ask the United States to stop the bombing unconditionally. Why? Here is a great power bombing a small nation with which it is not legally at war. It has been bombing that small nation for over one year killing its civilian men, women and children, laying waste its villages and destroying its crops. Surely it is not too much for Canada and for the other western powers to say to the United States: "In the hope that we can reconvene the conference, in the hope that we can begin negotiations toward peace, we want the bombing stopped".
The United States will not be making a concession because it discontinues the bombing. In my opinion it had no moral right to begin the bombing. It is not too much to ask that country now to discontinue, in the hope that the Geneva powers can be brought together, so that they can seek and find the solution to this conflict.
The second thing that will be necessary, if you get the Geneva powers together, is for the United States to state clearly, at this conference that it is prepared to negotiate not only with the government of North Viet Nam but also with the National Liberation Front in South Viet Nam. We may not like the
Interim Supply
National Liberation Front. We may not approve of its politics. The fact is that it represents over 50 per cent of the population, and occupies between 60 and 70 per cent of the territory of South Viet Nam.
The minister referred this afternoon to the National Liberation Front as "the insurgents". You will have some difficulty convincing the people in South Viet Nam that they are the insurgents, when what they sought to do was to obtain the benefits that were promised to them under the Geneva agreement. The people had been promised elections for July of 1956. They did not get them. The people had been promised that the demarcation line between North and South Viet Nam was a temporary line, and not to be considered a national boundary; that they were to have the right of self determination as to whether or not North and South Viet Nam would come together in a single and sovereign state; that they would have the right to determine what government they would have.
Instead of that they had a government foisted on them with United States bayonets, and maintained with United States financial and military power. The minister describes the people who object to this as insurgents. Whether or not they are insurgents, the fact is that there can be no hope of any solution until they are given a seat at the conference table, and until they have some voice in working out and negotiating a peace in South Viet Nam.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
There will be no peace in Viet Nam until all foreign troops are withdrawn. We recognize that to withdraw them without replacing them with some international peacekeeping force would probably introduce wholesale slaughter. A civil war cannot go on for more than ten years without a good deal of bitterness and hatred, as we saw even in Europe after the occupation by Nazi Germany. It therefore seems to me that, once the Geneva powers reach some basis of agreement between the conflicting parties, there will have to be an international police force supplied either by the Geneva accord powers or by the United Nations, stationed there for the purpose of maintaining law and order, for the purpose of supervising elections and for helping to set up a stable government in that war-torn country.
I readily concede that there is no easy solution. The minister is right when he says a solution cannot be found overnight. But this situation in Viet Nam has been going on for

Will the hon. member permit a question? He said the United States has been intervening for the last four years. Prior to that he said the government in South Viet Nam had been foisted upon them by American bayonets. Is it only in the last four years that there has been a government in South Viet Nam?

Oh no. As the hon. member knows, the so-called United States military advisors have been there, and military aid has been given to South Viet Nam ever since the Americans set up the well known Diem as a virtual dictator. However, the National Liberation Front which began to oppose Diem and his successors carried on guerilla warfare throughout the period from 1956 onward. But it is in the last four years that American intervention has been on a major scale. First it was military advisors. Then that pretext was brushed aside and the American forces which in 1964 numbered around 25,000 have been stepped up to a quarter of a million. Moreover, it is estimated that by next winter their strength will have reached 400,000.
Thus United States military participation has been growing steadily. It has ceased to be merely a small military effort buttressing that of the government. It has become a matter of America waging the war and the government of South Viet Nam merely going along for the ride.
The decision to intervene was made by President Kennedy.

That may be, but the decision to bomb North Viet Nam, the decision to escalate the war, the decision to raise the number of troops from 25,000 to 250,000, the decision to bomb Hanoi and Haiphong was taken by President Johnson who was elected in opposition to the very program which he is now carrying out. The Goldwater program which president Johnson opposed in 1964 is now being put into action by the man who opposed it.
Before I was interrupted I was saying that I do not suggest for a moment the solution is easy. When a conflict of this kind is allowed

to build up over a decade and when it is not possible to undo the past, it is naturally not easy to find a solution. But neither this government nor this parliament can continue to commit the crime of silence. We cannot stand silent while a war is being carried on, a large part of it directed against defenceless civilians. We cannot stand idly by while a war is being escalated to the point at which it may involve all mankind, without speaking out.
I had hoped that the minister would make today a clear and specific pronouncement as to where Canada stands. Instead, he contented himself by supporting the United States decision while at the same time regretting that we were in the mess we are in. In one breath he says there was no hope of a military solution and in the next he was saying there was not much use calling a conference.

Dear Sir:
With regards to the "speculation" on the part of certain persons concerning possible legislation by the Parliament of Canada on gang crews productivity or similar matters, our position is quite clear and unchanged.
Throughout mediation with Judge Rene Lippe, the various Ministers, or the Prime Minister of Canada, it was made clear as to terms that:
1.	We have not and we are not asking for any legislation, since we take the view that productivity in the above ports has continually increased;
2.	On the other hand, in the event that The Shipping Federation of Canada or others should ask for legislation, we do not join them or support them, either directly or indirectly;
3.	Should legislation be introduced in the Parliament of Canada on the request of the employers or otherwise, we will of course study the proposed legislation in order to determine our position. However, we will continue to oppose any final and binding arbitration, as we have throughout the negotiations and mediation and as shown in the "terms of settlement" wherein there is no reference to final and binding arbitration despite the various attempts of The Federation of Canada to include such terms;

I have received your letter of June 20 and appreciate your action in forwarding a copy of your letter of June 16 to Mr. Gerard Tremblay, Vice-President of the Atlantic Coast District of the International Longshoremen's Association.
In order to clear up any possible misunderstanding with respect to the settlement reached on June 14 between the International Longshoremen's Association Locals in Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec and The
Shipping Federation of Canada, there are a few observations which I would like to make on your letter to Mr. Tremblay.
During our discussions on June 13 and 14 and previously on June 11 and 12, both Mr. Pickersgill, who was the Acting Prime Minister in Mr. Pearson's absence over the weekend, and I stated that, provided the parties reached agreement on all of the other items in dispute, the government was prepared to establish an Industrial Inquiry Commission to carry out an independent and objective study of problems in connection with improvements in productivity, job security and related matters, and to take steps to have the conclusions reached as a result of this independent Industrial Inquiry Commission implemented by legislative enactment.
You will recall that the same commitment was made by the Prime Minister during the meetings held in his office on the night of June 13.
This commitment was directly associated throughout our discussions with the wage settlement for both 1966 and 1967 which, as you know, was only accepted by The Shipping Federation of Canada on the strength of this commitment.
It was also connected, you will recall, during our final discussions with the question of calling up and recalling of men.
You made it clear that the International Longshoremen's Association was not requesting the establishment of an Industrial Inquiry Commission or that legislation be introduced in this respect. You did say, however, that the International Longshoremen's Association would co-operate with the Industrial Inquiry Commission and that, if legislation were passed which provided for the implementation of the conclusions of this Commission through legislative enactment, the International Longshoremen's Association would not oppose the legislation and that you, as counsel for the International Longshoremen's Association, would advise that the law be respected.
The Terms of Settlement signed on June 14 include the following statement: "The agreements terminating on December 31, 1965, shall be amended by incorporating therein the terms of settlement set out above and these amended agreements shall remain in effect until December 31, 1967, unless amended by negotiations or otherwise." It was my understanding, and this has been confirmed by both Judge Lippe and Dr. Haythorne, that the words "or otherwise" were included to

Re your telegram June 30th apparently you were unaware of following facts Stop
When I.L.A. St. Lawrence river ports locals delegation left Montreal for Ottawa it was determined that no member of delegation would meet alone or without witnesses in seeing any minister or any representative of federal government Stop
While such an attitude may appear hostile it was the unanimous decision of the 18 delegates who having met with government representatives on two previous occasions in same dispute refused to go to Ottawa unless that rule be observed Stop
In fact no member of the delegation ever saw or spoke to any minister or government representative without being accompanied by Claude Jodoin, President, Canadian Labour Congress, Gerard Tremblay, I.L.A. VicePresident, Phil Cutler, one of the three attorneys present Stop
Furthermore, it was determined that the question of final and binding arbitration in all its aspects be left to President Jodoin as the spokesman on this issue Stop
At the very first meeting with several of your ministers when the Honourable Pick-ersgill put a question concerning final and binding arbitration to Phil Cutler, attorney, President Jodoin immediately and emphatically intervened to inform the various ministers present and all others that he, as Canadian Labour Congress President was mandated to reply and to state categorically that the I.L.A. was opposed to final and binding arbitration in any form as a settlement of this dispute and that Canadian Labour Congress supported this position of its affiliate as being identical to congress policy Stop
While we assume, Mr. Prime Minister, that you were not aware of the above facts, you will however recall that in your office and in your presence, the Honourable Nicholson raised the question of final and binding arbitration and again president Jodoin strenuously opposed final and binding arbitration being part of any settlement as a threat to free collective bargaining Stop
You may further recall, Mr. Prime Minister, that it was on that occasion that the Honourable MacEachen intervened concerning a recent speech he had made and assured president Jodoin and all others present that there was no decision on the part of the government to impose final and binding arbitration Stop
In any event, Mr. Prime Minister, since President Claude Jodoin was always present whenever any member of the I.L.A. delegation or any of the three accompanying attorneys met with you or other government representatives from the time we arrived in Ottawa until the time you, as Prime Minister, announced the settlement of the strike, we have communicated with President Jodoin and we understand that he will communicate with you so that knowledge of the facts be complete as to the reasons why the I.L.A. Right Honourable Lester B Pearson, Prime Minister of Cda
House of Commons Ottawa Ont As indicated to you during negotiations concerning the International Longshoremens Association I wish to reiterate to you that as a firm matter of policy the Canadian Labour Congress is unalterably opposed to any type of legislation indicating compulsory and binding arbitration. This type of legislation is completely contrary to democratic methods and to normal collective bargaining-
Claude Jodoin President CLC
July 8, 1966
